name: 07-sync-group
description: A synchronization group waits for its SLOWEST member -- and does not realign anything: it is a rendezvous, not a buffer. Three lanes: video written in real time (punctual until t=7s, then deliberately 2 frames late via pace.offset_ms), audio written in real time but only from t=4s, and a consumer asking one question, 'do you have data 300 ms from now?', of several groups over the same two readers. ASK 1 (video only) OK ~300 ms. ASK 2 (video+audio, audio silent) TOO_EARLY after the full 2000 ms deadline. ASK 3 (same group, audio removed) OK ~300 ms -- so audio was the blocker. ASK 4 (audio back and live, video punctual) OK ~304 ms, the baseline. ASK 5a exposes an SDK BUG: a group with more than one member stops synchronizing after its first successful wait and returns OK in 0.0003 ms (FlowSynchronizationGroup.cpp:112 misuses forward_list::splice_after). ASK 5b asks the identical question of a FRESH group and waits ~366 ms -- the laggard's 2 frames, absorbed. The exact proof is c14 vs c20: write lateness 0.238 ms -> 66.972 ms against 66.7334 ms injected, quantisation-free. c21/c22 show the two heads ~61 ms apart, which is why a consumer must address flows by TIMESTAMP, never by head.

A.note: VIDEO SOURCE. Runs in two phases: on time for the first 7 s, then deliberately 2 frames late.
seed the lane cursor at NOW, so grain indices line up with the wall clock
PHASE 1, ON TIME. pace, not delay_before_ms: the step sleeps until THIS grain's own OTS, so the flow sits exactly on the real-time grid. Each event reports late_ms (measured 0.013-9.7 ms).
210 grains x 33.37 ms = ~7 s of punctual video

PHASE 2, LATE BY EXACTLY 2 FRAMES. Same call, same cursor, same rate -- only pace.offset_ms changes: the step now sleeps until this grain's OTS PLUS 66.7334 ms (2 x 1001/30000 s) before writing it. The indices, and therefore the OTS, are unchanged; only the wall-clock moment of the commit moves. That is what a late source is.
75 grains x 33.37 ms = ~2.5 s of late video, t=7s to t=9.5s

B.note: AUDIO SOURCE. Deliberately silent for the first 4 s, then perfectly on time for the rest.
created NOW so lane C can open a reader on it; its head stays empty until b2 fires
THE SILENCE THAT DRIVES ASKS 1-3. Seeded after the wait, so audio starts at t=4s already in real time rather than racing to catch up.

480 samples = 10 ms at 48 kHz, which is the SDK'S OWN DEFAULT batch: for a continuous flow Instance.cpp:275 computes maxCommitBatchSizeHint as grainRate.numerator / (100 * denominator), i.e. 1/100 s. Writing in that unit is what a real producer does, and it also drops the audio member's commit granularity to 10 ms so the video's 66.7 ms lag is unmistakable. index is the EXCLUSIVE END, so this opens [cursor, cursor+480).
no range argument: the writer remembers what OpenSamples opened
550 batches x 10 ms = 5.5 s of audio, t=4s to t=9.5s

C.note: CONSUMER. One instance, two readers, two groups -- a group belongs to the instance that made it. The 500 ms wait matters: all lanes start together, and a reader cannot open a flow that does not exist yet. Without it c1/c2 fail with MXL_ERR_FLOW_NOT_FOUND, the AddReader steps have no reader, and the groups end up EMPTY -- and WaitForDataAt on an empty group returns MXL_STATUS_OK in 0.0002 ms, which looks like success.
video reader
audio reader -- succeeds even though the audio flow has no data yet
GROUP 1: video only. The control.
GROUP 2: video AND audio. The same video reader is a member of both groups.
AddReader waits for WHOLE grains; AddPartialGrainReader would wait for only N slices

ASK 1 - THE CONTROL. This step measures nothing interesting on its own; it exists to fix the yardstick BEFORE the failure, and to rule out the two boring explanations for it in advance. It establishes that ~300 ms is the right answer to this question at this instant (so ASK 2's 2000 and ASK 3's 302 mean something), that the timestamp expression below is sane, and that video is producing. When ASK 2 then blocks with the IDENTICAL expression, the only variable left is the audio member. EXPECT MXL_STATUS_OK, waited_ms ~300 (measured 293.5 / 294.0 / 300.3 / 305.8 / 306.4). THE SPREAD IS NOT SOFTWARE COST -- the group itself returns within ~28 us of the awaited grain's commit, measured. The variance is the media grid: timestampToIndex rounds to the NEAREST grain, so the grain actually waited for sits within +/-16.68 ms of the requested timestamp, and that phase is re-rolled every run because the cursor is seeded from 'current' at Run. Add a floor of ~0.31 ms, the median delay between a grain's OTS and its commit landing (pace wake + a 192 us fill of 5.5 MB + the commit): data is never available AT its OTS. A multi-member group adds the coarsest member's commit unit on top -- ASK 4 returned 6.25 ms after its video grain was already committed, waiting on audio's 10 ms batch boundary.
WHY edit_rate 1000000000/1 AND NOT THE VIDEO RATE: timestamp_ns is a TAI TIMESTAMP, not an index, but a scenario can only resolve INDEX expressions. timestampToIndex is (ts*num + 5e8*den)/(1e9*den), so a rate of 1000000000/1 makes one index exactly one nanosecond and 'mode: current' yields now-in-TAI-ns; the offset is then in ns. Passing the video rate here would resolve to a GRAIN index (~5.4e10) which, read as a timestamp, is 53 seconds after the epoch -- garbage. The per-flow conversion is the GROUP's job, not the scenario's: it takes this ONE timestamp and converts it with EACH member's own grainRate (FlowSynchronizationGroup.cpp:81). One timestamp, N rates -- that is the whole idea, and it is why the argument must not be pre-quantised to any single flow's grid.
WHY 300 ms AHEAD, and the ring: the lead is into the FUTURE, and ring depth constrains the PAST, so it does not collide with the 200 ms buffer depth. It is a demo device -- it makes the wait long enough to read off the log; production would ask for now, or slightly behind. The ring does bite on the other side: this video flow's ring is 5 grains = 167 ms (200 ms floored to whole grains), so once the wait returns you must read promptly. A consumer that waits for now+300 ms then dawdles 200 ms gets MXL_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE_TOO_LATE.
Event rows are stamped AFTER the call returns, so a wait appears in the log at its END.

ASK 2 - video + audio, same question, same instant, audio still silent. EXPECT MXL_ERR_OUT_OF_RANGE_TOO_EARLY, waited_ms ~2000 (measured 2000.07 / 2000.08) -- it burned the entire deadline waiting for the audio member. Say out loud: a timeout NEVER arrives as MXL_ERR_TIMEOUT, and the status does not name the member that was late. waited_ms against timeout_ns is the only tell.

Drop the audio member from group 2. NOTE THE CLOCK: there is no delay_before_ms on c10 or c11 -- the ~2 s that has passed since ASK 2 started is ASK 2's own timeout burning down. c9 blocked for its full 2000 ms deadline, so c10 and c11 run the moment it gives up.

ASK 3 - the same group GAV, now video-only, running immediately after ASK 2's deadline expired (that is where the ~2 s gap in the log comes from). EXPECT MXL_STATUS_OK, waited_ms ~300 (measured 302 / 302). Audio is STILL silent; the only thing that changed is the membership, which is what proves the audio reader was what blocked ASK 2.
put audio back

ASK 4 - video + audio, past t=4s so audio is live, and video is still in PHASE 1 (on time). EXPECT MXL_STATUS_OK, waited_ms 283-320 (measured 303.7 / 304.6). The spread is one video frame of quantisation: the wait ends when the grain NEAREST the target timestamp is committed, and that grain's own OTS sits anywhere within +/-16.7 ms of it. This is the BASELINE for ASK 5b.

BASELINE READ, the instant ASK 4 returned. Two numbers matter and only one of them is exact. age_ms (now - the head grain's OTS) carries the same frame quantisation as the wait: EXPECT 0-35 ms (measured 2.8-18.5). WRITE LATENESS = age_ms - stamp.transit_ms = write wall clock - OTS is quantisation-FREE, because both terms belong to the same grain: EXPECT ~0 (measured 0.238 ms). That is the number to compare against c20. It is the same column M15's timing panel shows.

ASK 5a - THE BUG, and why the next step exists. Same group as ASK 4, video now 2 frames late, so this should wait LONGER than ASK 4. It returns MXL_STATUS_OK in ~0.0003 ms instead. A synchronization group with MORE THAN ONE member stops synchronizing after its first successful wait: FlowSynchronizationGroup.cpp:112 calls _readers.splice_after(before_begin, _readers, current), but forward_list::splice_after moves the element FOLLOWING the iterator, not the iterator's own element -- and when current is the last member that is undefined behaviour. A single-member group never reaches that branch, which is why GV (ASK 1) keeps working all day. Failing by returning OK instantly is the worst shape a bug can take: it looks like success.
WORKAROUND: a pristine group. Same two readers, same question, same instant -- the only difference is that this one has never completed a wait.

ASK 5b - THE LATE-SOURCE CASE, on the fresh group. Identical to ASK 4 except that video has been 2 frames late since t=7s. EXPECT MXL_STATUS_OK, waited_ms 350-385 (measured 366.4) against ASK 4's 283-320. THE GROUP HELD THE CONSUMER FOR EXACTLY AS LONG AS THE LAGGARD NEEDED. The two ranges cannot overlap, and the gap between them IS the lag -- but read a single pair of numbers carefully, because each carries +/-16.7 ms of frame quantisation. c14 vs c20 measures the same lag exactly. And put ASK 5a beside this: same members, same question, same second -- 0 ms from the used group, 366 ms from the correct one.

THE SAME READ AS c14, 2 s later, and THE PROOF. age_ms 67-100 (measured 67.03). WRITE LATENESS measured 66.972 ms against c14's 0.238 -- a difference of 66.734 ms against the 66.7334 ms injected into a6's pace.offset_ms. Six TENTHS of a microsecond from exactly 2 frames, with no quantisation anywhere in it. Nothing about the reader, the call or the index changed, and the OTS is still derived from the grain index; what moved is only WHEN the writer committed it.
SKEW, HALF ONE: the TAI timestamp the VIDEO head represents. Result field is ots_ns.

SKEW, HALF TWO: the same for the AUDIO head. Subtract c21's ots_ns from c22's: measured 60.3-62.7 ms, i.e. the 2-frame lag less each flow's own commit granularity (video 33.4 ms, audio now 10 ms). YES -- this is the answer to 'are the two heads 2 frames apart': they are, and that is the point. The two flows' newest data is NOT contemporaneous, so a consumer that simply reads both heads is 2 frames out of sync. A sync group does not move these heads together -- NOTHING does, and nothing buffers or reorders a payload. It tells you WHEN a timestamp YOU chose is present in every member, so you address every flow by that one timestamp instead of by its head. For an exact, quantisation-free figure use c14 vs c20 instead.
and audio is readable at once -- after ASK 5b returned, BOTH members have data at the timestamp. EXPECT MXL_STATUS_OK with no wait.
tidy up: releasing a group does not touch its readers
five of the six syncgroup calls appear in this scenario; only AddPartialGrainReader does not
